content: Individuals with cystic fibrosis (CF) who also have pancreatic insufficiency are at an increased risk of developing deficiencies in fat-soluble vitamins, including vitamin A. A deficiency in vitamin A can primarily lead to problems with vision and skin health. However, excessive levels of vitamin A can be harmful, particularly in children, as it may negatively impact the respiratory and skeletal systems and interfere with the metabolism of other fat-soluble vitamins. To address this, many CF treatment centers routinely provide vitamin A supplements to reduce the risk of deficiency and to improve clinical outcomes, such as growth. However, the recommended dosage of vitamin A supplementation varies across different clinical guidelines. A systematic review of vitamin A and related compounds (such as carotenes or other retinoids) in individuals with CF could provide valuable guidance for clinical practice. This review is an update of a previous Cochrane Review. The objective of this review was to determine whether supplementation with vitamin A, carotenes, or other retinoid compounds in children and adults with CF reduces the occurrence of vitamin A deficiency-related disorders, improves overall and respiratory health, and influences the risk of vitamin A toxicity. To conduct this review, researchers searched the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group Trials Register, which includes data from electronic databases and manual searches of journals and conference abstracts. Additional searches were conducted in ongoing trial registries, such as ClinicalTrials.gov, the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, and the International Standard Randomised Controlled Trial Number Registry. The most recent database search was performed on June 1, 2018. The review included all randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared any form of oral vitamin A, carotene, or retinoid supplementation (alone or in combination) to a placebo. The studies had to involve supplementation for at least three months in individuals with CF (diagnosed via sweat tests or genetic testing), with or without pancreatic insufficiency. Two authors independently assessed the quality of the studies and extracted data on outcomes. The quality of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE system. Investigators were contacted to obtain any missing quantitative data. No studies specifically investigating vitamin A or other retinoid supplementation met the inclusion criteria. However, one randomized study involving 24 individuals with CF who were receiving pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy was included. This study examined the effects of beta (β)-carotene supplementation. Participants underwent two successive supplementation periods: a high-dose phase followed by a low-dose phase, both compared to a placebo. However, the results from the low-dose phase should be interpreted cautiously due to the absence of a wash-out period after the high-dose phase. The study did not report on two of the primary outcomes of the review: vitamin A deficiency-related disorders and mortality. For the third primary outcome, growth and nutritional status (measured as the z-score for height), there was no significant difference between the supplementation and placebo groups. The mean difference (MD) was -0.23 (95% confidence interval [CI] -0.89 to 0.43), and the evidence was of low quality. Regarding secondary outcomes, high-dose β-carotene supplementation for three months resulted in significantly fewer days of systemic antibiotic use to treat pulmonary exacerbations compared to the placebo group (MD -15 days, 95% CI -27.60 to -2.40). However, this benefit was not sustained during the second three-month period when the β-carotene dose was reduced (MD -8 days, 95% CI -18.80 to 2.80). The evidence for these findings was of low quality. There were no statistically significant differences between the groups in terms of lung function, and no adverse events were reported. The evidence for these outcomes was also of low quality. Supplementation increased plasma β-carotene levels but did not affect vitamin A levels. The study did not assess quality of life or vitamin A toxicity. The authors concluded that, due to the lack of randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials on retinoid supplementation, no definitive conclusions can be drawn regarding the use of vitamin A supplementation in individuals with CF. Furthermore, the methodological limitations of the included study, as reflected in the low-quality evidence assessed using the GRADE system, prevent any clear conclusions about β-carotene supplementation. Until more robust data become available, clinicians should adhere to countryor region-specific guidelines for vitamin A and related supplementation practices in CF management.
